title: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

relationships.phenotype: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis, also called intermediate cystinosis, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene (606272) on chromosome 17p13.2.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis, also called intermediate cystinosis, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract says intermediate cystinosis results from compound heterozygous or homozygous CTNS mutations.

checks.claim: The CTNS gene is located on chromosome 17p13.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations of CTNS causing intermediate cystinosis.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene named in the paper.

paragraphs.text: Late-onset (intermediate) cystinosis is a rare form of cystinosis. It is milder than the infantile nephropathic form. Attard et al. (1999) described symptoms beginning between 12 and 15 years of age. Thoene et al. (1999) found that the disease arose from 1 mild CTNS mutation combined with 1 mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or from homozygosity for a mutation predicted to be mild.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) described late-onset cystinosis as a rarer form of the disorder, with symptoms beginning between 12 and 15 years of age. They studied 2 late-onset patients whose phenotype was milder than infantile nephropathic cystinosis. They also studied 3 patients whose cystinosis began before 7 years of age but whose course was milder than the infantile nephropathic form.

paragraphs.text: In 6 patients with intermediate cystinosis, Thoene et al. (1999) identified mutations in the CTNS gene, 2 of which had not been described before. The disease resulted either from 1 mild mutation combined with 1 mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis (compound heterozygosity) or from homozygosity for a mutation predicted to be mild. Thoene et al. (1999) transfected cystinotic fibroblasts with normal CTNS cDNA or with a cDNA carrying a mutation that causes intermediate cystinosis. Both partially corrected the cells' phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) found CTNS mutations in 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis. The mutations affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin, which the authors said accounted for the milder phenotype. In 3 patients whose disease began before 7 years of age but followed a milder course than infantile nephropathic cystinosis, they found missense mutations. They suggested these mutations allow production of functional protein.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) found 23 different CTNS mutations, 14 of them novel, in patients with infantile nephropathic, late-onset, and atypical cystinosis. They had 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis. Of these, 12 had 2 severely truncating mutations, consistent with loss of functional protein. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions, which the authors predicted would disrupt transmembrane domains and abolish protein function. In contrast, the mutations in 2 late-onset patients affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin, accounting for their milder phenotype. In 3 patients with onset before 7 years of age and a milder course, the missense mutations were suggested to allow production of functional protein.
